en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 13.1 (SN 13.1, PTS SN ii 133) 1. Chapter on Realization: The Discourse on the Tip of a Finger [The Buddha said: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take up a single grain of dust from the tip of his finger and say: ‘This is more than the earth,’ would he be speaking truthfully? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take up a single grain of dust from the tip of his finger and say: ‘This is more than the water in the great ocean,’ would he be speaking truthfully? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take up a single grain of dust from the tip of his finger and say: ‘This is more than the sand in the Ganges River,’ would he be speaking truthfully? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take up a single grain of dust from the tip of his finger and say: ‘This is more than the grass, shrubs, trees, and herbs on this great earth,’ would he be speaking truthfully? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take up a single grain of dust from the tip of his finger and say: ‘This is more than the blood shed by beings in this world who have been born and have died,’ would he be speaking truthfully? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take up a single grain of dust from the tip of his finger and say: ‘This is more than the tears shed by beings in this world who have been born and have died,’ would he be speaking truthfully? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to take up a single grain of dust from the tip of his finger and say: ‘This is more than the mother’s milk drunk by beings in this world who have been born and have died,’ would he be speaking truthfully? “No, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been one’s mother, or one’s father, or one’s brother, or one’s sister, or one’s son, or one’s daughter. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been killed by you, or whose flesh you have eaten. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your enemy, or whose head you have cut off. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your relative or your friend, or whose death you have caused, or whose property you have seized. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your wife, or whose body you have violated. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your husband, or whose body you have violated. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your child or whose life you have taken. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your teacher or whose instructions you have rejected. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your preceptor or whose instructions you have rejected. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your companion or whose instructions you have rejected. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your fellow monk or whose instructions you have rejected. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your mother, father, brother, sister, son, or daughter. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your enemy, or whose head you have cut off. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your relative or friend, or whose death you have caused, or whose property you have seized. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Ignorance is the cause of this. “Bhikkhus, it is not easy to find a being who has not, in the course of saṃsāra, been your wife, or whose body you have violated. For such a long time, bhikkhus, beings have undergone suffering, experienced pain, endured anguish, and wandered in saṃsāra. And what is the cause of this? Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the Blessed One, having placed a tiny amount of dust on the tip of his fingernail, addressed the bhikkhus:
“What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more:
this little bit of dust that I have placed on the tip of my fingernail, or this great earth?
“Venerable sir, this great earth alone is more; it is far more than that little bit of dust.”
“Very little indeed, monks, has been placed by the Blessed One upon the tip of his fingernail—a mere speck of dust.

It does not approach a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of the great earth compared to that tiny speck of dust placed by the Blessed One upon the tip of his fingernail.

“In the same way, monks, for a noble disciple who is accomplished in view, a person who has realized the truth, this very suffering that has been exhausted and eliminated is far more abundant [than what remains].”
What remains is trifling.

It does not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part of the previous mass of suffering that has been exhausted and brought to an end—namely, the limit of seven more existences at most.
Thus, monks, the breakthrough to the Dhamma is of great benefit.
"Thus, the acquisition of the Dhamma-eye is of great benefit.
Thus was the first [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 13.2 (SN 13.2, PTS SN ii 133).
1. The Chapter on Clear Comprehension (Abhisamaya-vagga). The Lotus Pond Discourse (Pokkharaṇī-sutta).
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a lotus pond fifty yojanas in length, fifty yojanas in width, and fifty yojanas in depth, full of water, brimming so that a crow could drink from it.
Then a man would draw up some water with the tip of a blade of kusa grass.
What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“Which is more: the water drawn up by the tip of a blade of kusa grass, or the water in the lotus pond?
“Venerable sir, this alone is more: the water in the lotus pond.
The water drawn up by the tip of a blade of kusa grass is trifling.”
“Compared to the water in the lotus pond, the water drawn up by a blade of kusa grass does not come even within a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part.

“In the same way, monks, for a noble disciple who is accomplished in view and has realized the truth, this suffering that has been exhausted and eliminated is far more vast, while what remains is trifling.”

"It does not approach even a hundredth part, it does not approach even a thousandth part, it does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part of the previous mass of suffering that has been exhausted and brought to an end, namely, the state of being limited to seven more births at most.
Thus, monks, the breakthrough to the Dhamma is of great benefit; thus, the acquisition of the eye of the Dhamma is of great benefit.
This is the second [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 13.3 1. Abhisamaya Vagga Sambhejja-udaka Sutta: The Confluence of Waters “Bhikkhus, suppose there were two streams of water flowing together from opposite directions, and a man would come along bringing a large boat. He would fasten a rudder to the stern and a pole to the prow, and he would go upstream against the current. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that man be able to go upstream against the current by his own strength? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, so too, when a noble disciple possesses four things, it is fitting for him to declare: ‘I understand as it really is: “This is suffering”; I understand as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”; I understand as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; I understand as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. What are the four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. Possessing these four things, bhikkhus, it is fitting for a noble disciple to declare: ‘I understand as it really is: “This is suffering” ... “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Just as, bhikkhus, when two streams of water flow together from opposite directions, and a man comes along bringing a large boat, fastens a rudder to the stern and a pole to the prow, and goes upstream against the current—he can indeed go upstream against the current by his own strength; so too, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, it is fitting for him to declare: ‘I understand as it really is: “This is suffering” ... “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”’”
At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, it is just as if there were these great rivers—the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—which converge and meet together;
suppose a man were to draw up two or three drops of water from them.
“What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more:

those two or three drops of water that have been drawn out, or the water in the confluence?”— “Venerable sir, the water in the confluence is far more, compared to those two or three drops of water that have been drawn out.”
“Those two or three drops of water that have been removed are trifling;
they do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, when compared with the water of the confluence.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, ...pe...”
“The acquisition of the eye of Dhamma.
Third.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 13.4 (SN 13.4, PTS SN ii 133)
1. The Chapter on Clear Realization.
The Second Discourse on Water Mixed Together.
[The Blessed One] was staying at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were these great rivers—the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—which converge and flow together;
suppose that water were to reach its exhaustion and total depletion, with the exception of two or three drops.
What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“Which, then, is more: the water in the confluence that has been exhausted and consumed, or the two or three drops of water that remain?
“Venerable sir, this very water in the confluence that has been exhausted and consumed is far more;
the two or three drops of water that remain are negligible.”

“Compared to the water that has been mixed together, exhausted, and completely consumed, those two or three drops of water remaining do not come to even a hundredth part, they do not come to even a thousandth part, they do not come to even a hundred-thousandth part.
“In the same way, monks, ... [as above] ...”
“the attainment of the Dhamma-eye.
Fourth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 13.5 (SN 13.5, PTS SN ii 136)
1. Abhisamaya Chapter:
The Discourse on the Earth.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was staying.
“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to place seven pellets the size of jujube stones upon the great earth.
What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more:
those seven pellets the size of jujube stones that have been placed there, or the great earth?”
“Venerable sir, this very great earth is far more;
the seven pellets the size of jujube stones placed beside it are insignificant.
Compared to the great earth, the seven pellets the size of jujube stones do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part.”
“In the same way, monks … [as before] … the attainment of the Dhamma-eye.
The fifth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 13.6 (SN 13.6, PTS SN ii 136) 1. Abhisamaya-vagga The Second Discourse on the Earth At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great mass of earth extending an hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas. Then a man would come along, desiring to see the world’s end, seeking the world’s end, thinking: ‘Where is the world’s end? Where is the limit of the world? After traveling for a long time, he would take a handful of that great mass of earth and throw it far away, thinking: ‘I have brought this handful of earth from the world’s end. Then, a second person would come along, desiring to see the world’s end... [and so on with a third, fourth, and fifth person]. Then, a sixth person would come along, desiring to see the world’s end, seeking the world’s end, thinking: ‘Where is the world’s end? Where is the limit of the world? After traveling for a long time, he would take up that handful of earth thrown away by the first person and throw it even further away, thinking: ‘I have brought this handful of earth from the world’s end. What do you think, bhikkhus? Which is greater: the handful of earth thrown away by that person, or the great mass of earth? “It is the great mass of earth, Blessed One; it is the great mass of earth, Fortunate One. The handful of earth thrown away by that person is trifling; it is not even a fraction, nor a counting, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor an analogy to the great mass of earth. “So too, bhikkhus, for one who has abandoned the five lower fetters, there is no measure to the extent of his rebirths in the various realms of existence. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that is the very nature of things. For one who has abandoned the five lower fetters, there is no measure to the extent of his rebirths in the various realms of existence. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great mass of water extending an hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas. Then a man would come along, desiring to see the world’s end... [as above]...

Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great stone mountain extending an hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas. Then a man would come along, desiring to see the world’s end... [as above]... Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great tree extending an hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas. Then a man would come along, desiring to see the world’s end... [as above]... Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great heap of grain extending an hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas. Then a man would come along, desiring to see the world’s end... [as above]... Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great heap of chaff extending an hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas. Then a man would come along, desiring to see the world’s end... [as above]... Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great heap of sawdust extending an hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas. Then a man would come along, desiring to see the world’s end... [as above]... Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great heap of ashes extending an hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas, or four hundred yojanas. Then a man would come along, desiring to see the world’s end... [as above]... So too, bhikkhus, for one who has abandoned the five lower fetters, there is no measure to the extent of his rebirths in the various realms of existence. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that is the very nature of things. For one who has abandoned the five lower fetters, there is no measure to the extent of his rebirths in the various realms of existence.”
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Bhikkhus, suppose the great earth were to be exhausted and consumed, with the exception of seven pellets the size of jujube stones.
What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“Which is more: that portion of the great earth which has been worn away and consumed, or the seven small pellets remaining, each the size of a jujube seed?
“Venerable sir, this much of the great earth that has been worn away and consumed is far more;
the seven small pellets remaining, each the size of a jujube seed, are trifling.”

“Compared to the great earth that has been exhausted and consumed, those seven pellets the size of jujube seeds that remain do not come to even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part.
“In the same way, monks, [compared to the suffering of saṃsāra], the attainment of the eye of Dhamma does not come to even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part.”
Sixth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 13.7 (SN 13.7, PTS SN ii 136) 1.
Abhisamaya-vagga (The Chapter on Realization)
The Discourse on the Ocean. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to draw up two or three drops of water from the great ocean. [What do you think, bhikkhus?]”
"What do you think, monks, which is more:
those two or three drops of water that have been removed, or the water in the great ocean?
"Venerable sir, the water in the great ocean is far more; it is immeasurable."
“Those two or three drops of water that have been drawn out are insignificant;
they do not bear even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part of the water in the great ocean compared to those two or three drops that have been drawn out.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, ... [and so on].”
“The attainment of the Dhamma-eye.
The seventh [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 13.8 (SN 13.8, PTS SN ii 137).
1. The Chapter on Clear Realization (Abhisamayavagga). The Second Discourse on the Ocean (Dutiyasamuddasutta).
[The Blessed One] was staying at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, suppose the great ocean were to undergo depletion and exhaustion, with the exception of two or three drops of water.
What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more:
the water in the great ocean that has been depleted and exhausted, or the two or three drops of water that remain?”
“Venerable sir, that water in the great ocean which has been exhausted and consumed is far more;
the two or three drops of water remaining are insignificant.
They do not amount to a hundredth part, they do not amount to a thousandth part, nor do they amount to a hundred-thousandth part.”
“Just as when the water in the great ocean has been exhausted and consumed, only two or three drops of water remain,” [the Blessed One said].
“In the same way, monks, … [as before] … the acquisition of the eye of Dhamma.”
The Eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 13.9 (SN 13.9, PTS SN ii 137) 1.
Abhisamaya-vagga (The Chapter on Realization)
The Mountain Discourse.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to set down seven grains of gravel, each the size of a mustard seed, at the foot of Himavat, the king of mountains.
“What do you think, monks, which is more:
those seven mustard-seed-sized pebbles that have been set down, or the Himalayas, the king of mountains?
“Venerable sir, the Himalayas, the king of mountains, is far more numerous.”
“Seven tiny pebbles, each the size of mustard seeds, have been set down.

They do not approach even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of the Himalayas, the king of mountains, compared to those seven mustard-seed-sized pebbles that have been set down.
“In the same way, …pe…”
“the attainment of the eye of Dhamma.
The ninth [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 13.10 (SN 13.10, PTS SN ii 138)
1. The Chapter on Clear Comprehension (Abhisamaya-vagga). The Second Discourse on Mountains (Pabbata-sutta).
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Bhikkhus, suppose the Himalayas, the king of mountains, were to be worn away and exhausted, with the exception of seven grains of gravel the size of mustard seeds.
What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more:
that portion of the Himalayas, the king of mountains, which has been worn away and exhausted, or those seven grains of gravel the size of mustard seeds that remain?”
“Venerable sir, it is precisely that which has been worn away and consumed from Himavat, the king of mountains, that is more;
the seven mustard seeds the size of pebbles remaining are insignificant.
They do not amount to a hundredth part, they do not amount to a thousandth part, they do not amount to a hundred-thousandth part.”
“Compared to the Himalayas, the king of mountains, which has been completely exhausted and consumed, only seven pebble-sized grains of mustard seed remain.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple, a person accomplished in view who has realized the truth, that suffering which has been completely exhausted and consumed is vast,
while what remains is trifling.”

"It does not approach even a hundredth part, it does not approach even a thousandth part, it does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part of the former mass of suffering that has been exhausted and brought to an end, compared with this state of being limited to seven more births at most.
So great, monks, is the benefit of the breakthrough to the Dhamma; so great is the benefit of the acquisition of the eye of Dhamma. Tenth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 13.11 1. Abhisamaya Vagga Tatiyapabbata Sutta: The Third Discourse on Mountains “Bhikkhus, there are these three mountains that are unshakable and immovable. What three? The mountain of gold, the mountain of silver, and the mountain of crystal. These are the three mountains that are unshakable and immovable. In the same way, bhikkhus, there are these three mountains that are unshakable and immovable. What three? The mountain of the Dhamma, the mountain of the Vinaya, and the mountain of the Teaching. These are the three mountains that are unshakable and immovable.”
At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to set down seven pebbles the size of mung beans upon Sineru, the king of mountains.
What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“Which now is more: these seven pebble-grains the size of mung beans that have been set down, or Sineru, the king of mountains?
“Venerable sir, this very Sineru, the king of mountains, is far more;
those seven pebble-grains the size of mung beans that have been set down are insignificant.”

“They do not come within a hundredth part, they do not come within a thousandth part, they do not come within a hundred-thousandth part of Sineru, the king of mountains, when seven pebbles the size of mung beans are set beside it. “In the same way, bhikkhus,
when the attainment of a noble disciple who is accomplished in view is compared to the attainment of recluses,
brahmins, and wanderers of other sects, theirs does not come within a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part...”
It does not approach even a hundred-thousandth part [of the merit].
Thus great is the attainment, bhikkhus, of a person accomplished in view; thus great is his direct knowledge.
The eleventh.
The Connected Discourses on Clear Comprehension (Abhisamayasaṃyutta) is completed.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
The Finger-Nail Tip and the Lotus Pond.
And two [are] like mingled water;
two are like earth, two like the ocean,
and three are like mountains.
